summary: Deep dive into tenancy options (vGPU/MIG vs dedicated), KV cache hotspotting, eviction policies, and quantization trade-offs for AstraCloud's latency-sensitive assistant. Agreed to run KV hotspot benchmark and follow up with quantization POC and network walkthrough.
topics: Tenancy isolation options; noisy neighbor mitigation; KV cache eviction and hot-key handling; batching/continuous batching; quantization impact on latency and quality; VPC/on-prem networking constraints; fallback routing and SLO design
transcript:
[00:00] Liam (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we've got Maya, Jonas, Li Wei from AstraCloud, and Priya and Omar from my side. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Maya (AstraCloud - Platform Lead): Good thanks, Liam. Excited to get into this — we've been hitting some odd tail latency during peak for the assistant.
[00:22] Jonas (AstraCloud - Infra): Yeah morning, we saw this when a specific customer traffic pattern hit a single prefix, KV cache syst— the kv-cache was basically thrashing.
[00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): Okay, that's exactly what we wanted to dig into. We'll cover tenancy options first then dig into KV hot keys, eviction and quantization.
[00:42] [00:45] Omar (Redwood SRE): Quick ask — please do mention the traffic shapes (qps, seq len) so we can map to batching behavior.
[00:50] Li Wei (AstraCloud - ML): We'll share histograms, yes. But to frame it: single-tenant traffic is mixed, there are a few heavy customers that generate long sequences and lots of repeated prefixes.
[01:05] Liam: Cool. High level: dedicated GPUs give you the strongest isolation vs hosted multi-tenant where you can get noisy neighbor effects unless you use tenancy tech like MIG, vGPU, or capacity fencing. The trade is cost and utilization.
[01:20] Jonas: Can you explain MIG vs vGPU in practice? We saw both terms but not sure differences in interference.
[01:26] Priya: Sure — MIG partitions physical GPU into slices, pretty good for strict isolation of memory and compute. vGPU can multiplex more flexibly but has shared scheduler and can induce contention under burst. Also, some kernel paths behave differently (NCCL, custom kernels) and that can cause tail spikes.
[01:45] Maya: So for our use-case (latency SLO 95th < 450ms) dedicated sounds safer, but cost wise it's ... high. Any middle ground?
[01:56] Priya: Yes, hybrid model — dedicated for top-tier customers or low-latency routes, hosted for others with fallback policies. Redwood's routing can do policy-based routing per route or per token cost band.
[02:10] [02:15] Jonas: That fallback routing — what happens on capacity pressure? Do requests queue, get routed to slower model, or fail?
[02:20] Omar: Our typical pattern is graceful degrade: route to quantized variant or smaller model; if that still fails, failover to another region or reserved capacity. We don't queue in a way that blocks client, we keep timeouts client-configurable.
[02:36] Li Wei: About KV cache — we saw when a hot prefix gets evicted, there's a big spike. Is that expected?
[02:43] Priya: Yes, cold KV cache warm-up cost is real. When a hot key is evicted and then gets traffic again, you pay the full compute to rehydrate prefix/kvs. Two mitigations: anti-entropy replication across nodes (costly), and smarter eviction like LFU with hot-key pinning or sticky caching for certain routes.
[03:05] Maya: We were thinking of pinning top 200 prefixes for our largest customers. Does that make sense?
[03:10] Priya: It can. But watch memory vs throughput tradeoff. If pinning consumes too much KV memory, you'll reduce the effective model concurrency and lower throughput. Best to run a hotspot benchmark to quantify.
[03:24] [03:30] Liam: We'll provide the benchmark harness. It simulates qps per prefix distribution and measures rehydration latency and tail percentiles, and also memory footprint.
[03:39] Jonas: Great. Can it simulate eviction policies? We use LRU now, but LFU might be better.
[03:44] Priya: Yes, our harness can toggle LRU/LFU/TinyLFU and pin sets. We'll include a recommended config for AstraCloud.
[03:52] Li Wei: What about batching and continuous batching - we've seen some odd interactions with long sequences beating short sequences.
[03:58] Omar: Continuous batching aims to preserve latency SLO by dynamically forming micro-batches. But batch formation depends on seq length distribution; long sequences can monopolize the batch window.
[04:12] Priya: One pattern is preemptible micro-batches: short requests get fast paths with small batches; long ones get scheduled on reserved slots. That reduces tail for short queries.
[04:24] Maya: Sounds like we need per-route or per-API policies — can Redwood do that?
[04:29] Liam: Yes, per-route policies and route tags. You can configure latency targets and Redwood will adjust batching windows and routing.
[04:36] [04:40] Jonas: Quantization: we tested int8, saw 2-3x throughput but a small quality drop on instruction-following. Is there a middle ground?
[04:48] Priya: Mixed precision or MSE-aware quantization can help. int8 symmetric/uniform is fast but sometimes degrades logits for some heads. 4-bit quant can be surprising — great density but you need calibration and some models require per-channel quant.
[05:02] Li Wei: Do you have automatic quality regression hooks? We need to prevent hallucination regressions during rollout.
[05:08] Priya: Redwood Optimize has eval hooks — run your golden prompt set and compare key metrics (BLEU/EM/LLR or domain-specific checks). We alert on regressions and can auto-roll back.
[05:19] Maya: In an on-prem deployment, are there constraints for quantization - like does GPU driver support matter?
[05:25] Priya: Yes, driver and library support matters (cuBLAS, CUTLASS, custom kernels). For on-prem, we'll need to match kernel versions; some quant kernels use specialized fused ops that require particular CUDA/cuDNN versions.
[05:38] [05:45] Jonas: For noisy neighbor mitigation on hosted, have you seen success with KV-aware scheduling?
[05:51] Omar: We experimented with KV-aware packing — avoid co-locating tenants with high KV working sets on same instance. That requires a placement scheduler that knows memory working set and expected seq lengths. It's effective but needs accurate signals.
[06:06] Li Wei: How do you get those signals? From recent telemetry?
[06:09] Priya: Yes, token-level telemetry, recent working set histograms, and rolling-window hot-key detection. Redwood Console surfaces per-route cache hit rates and per-token latency so you can make placement decisions.
[06:22] Maya: On the security side, if we do Private VPC with on-prem connectors, how is KV stored and encrypted?
[06:29] Liam: We support in-cluster KV with customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. Keys never leave your control plane in Private deployments; for hosted, we offer KMS integrations and envelope encryption. Audit logs are available.
[06:40] Jonas: Network paths worry us — cold starts when connecting to hosted control plane add latency. We need offline or local control plane for on-prem?
[06:48] Omar: For strict environments we provide an optional private control plane or air-gapped packaging. That eliminates the control-plane round-trip; only telemetry can be optionally latched and forwarded through approved channels.
[06:59] [07:05] Li Wei: Back to eviction — is it feasible to implement a hybrid: pin top N prefixes and use probabilistic cache for rest?
[07:11] Priya: Totally feasible. It's actually common: pin the top heavy-hitters and use a tiny-LFU for the rest with expiration windows tuned to your access pattern. The trick is tuning on memory and churn.
[07:24] Jonas: What are the instrumentation costs? Extra metrics, memory overhead?
[07:29] Priya: Tiny-LFU needs a small sketch per entry; memory overhead is modest (a few percent) but you must measure. We'll include instrumentation toggles in the harness.
[07:39] Maya: For the pilot, what would success look like?
[07:43] Liam: Reduce 95th latency by at least 30% during peak, and keep cache rehydration events under a target rate. Plus a validated quantized POC with <X% quality regression on golden prompts.
[07:57] Li Wei: What X% do you normally recommend?
[08:00] Priya: Depends on metric — for instruction-following we often target <2% relative drop on domain evals. For embeddings maybe tighter. We'll advise per-metric thresholds.
[08:12] [08:15] Jonas: Regarding throughput guarantees if we buy Dedicated — what SLA can we expect vs hosted?
[08:21] Liam: Dedicated comes with capacity commitments and SLA-backed throughput. You get reserved GPU pools and predictable p99 tail latencies based on reserved capacity. Hosted has soft SLOs but we offer reserved dedicated nodes for strict needs.
[08:36] Maya: How do we test noisy neighbor scenarios before committing?
[08:39] Priya: The benchmark harness can simulate co-tenancy, injecting background traffic to measure tail and jitter. We recommend running that in a staging cluster identical to your prod config.
[08:52] [09:00] Jonas: One last thing — cold KV rehydration cost: can we pre-warm on deploy?
[09:05] Omar: Yes, pre-warm is possible; we also support lazy pre-fetch to warm top N prefixes during deploy. But that increases deploy time and memory.
[09:15] Maya: Okay great. Let's talk timelines.
[09:18] Liam: Next week Redwood will send the harness and a suggested config. Priya will add quantization playbook. Maya to schedule network walkthrough.
[09:27] Li Wei: Quick note — we have compliance constraints, SOC2 and customer data never leaves region. Need to validate region controls.
[09:33] Liam: Noted — we'll include data residency notes and region routing.
[09:38] [09:45] Jonas: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[09:48] Maya: Thanks.
[09:50] Priya: One minute — I'll also add a suggested eviction config and a sample tiny-LFU config to the follow up.
[09:57] Liam: Perfect. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the bench run. Meeting adjourned.
[10:00] End of recording.
